name: Meru
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Moehlig, Wilhelm J. G. (1974), dialect study of Meru varieties (cited on Glottolog meru1245); Bantu descriptive work plausibly covering prosody

new_statements.quote: H(igh) tone is marked by an acute accent (´) and L(ow) tone is unmarked. A raised H tone is marked with a double acute accent ( ̋ ), while the symbol ˚ indicates that a prepausal L is realized with a level pitch rather than the default prepausal low fall (cf. Ford 1976). [...] With a few exceptions, prepenultimate long vowels are shortened in Tiania: o‑tó-saal-a 'to choose us' vs. o-tó-sal-er-a 'to choose for us'. In addition, a vowel followed by a nasal+consonant (NC) complex lengthens in penultimate position, but not prepenultimately. Hence /tɔng/ 'touch' o-tɔɔnga 'to touch', o-tɔng-an-a 'to touch each other'.
new_statements.citation: Hyman, Larry M. & Mwaambi G. Mbûûi. 2022. Dahl's law and g-deletion in Tiania: A dialect of Kimeru (Bantu, Kenya). Language in Africa 3(2): 212-238. doi:10.37892/2686-8946-2022-3-2-212-238
new_statements.locator: p. 214 n. 2 (tone) and p. 221 n. 5 (penultimate length)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Meru is a two-level (H/L) tone language with lexically and grammatically distinctive tone; no source opened states a word-stress rule. The only prominence-related statement is positional: in Tiania long vowels survive only in the penultimate syllable (prepenultimate long vowels shorten; NC-lengthening applies only in the penult), i.e. a penultimate-length effect, not a stress rule. Ford 1976 (p. 261, 267) states that in all Central Kenya Bantu dialects examined, including Imenti, Tigania and Miitine, 'tone is both lexically distinctive and serves to reinforce particular aspects of syntax', with two basic tone levels expandable to four (extra-high/extra-low) at syntactic boundaries.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Hyman & Mbûûi 2022 n. 5: 'with a few exceptions' prepenultimate long vowels shorten; n. 11 (p. 232): a CVVC root keeps its length before the short habitual -a, suggesting the root syllable counts as penultimate within a smaller domain. Taitumu 2014 (MA thesis on word formation, p. 12) asserts in passing that in a newly coined Kimeru noun 'stress is placed on the first syllable of the new naming unit' (mwitithiangari 'vehicle driver'); this is an unargued illustration of Štekauer's onomasiological model, not a phonological description, and no other source supports initial stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Verb and noun forms in isolation and in sentence context (Tiania); tone marking conventions are at word level with prepausal (utterance-final) effects. Gacunku 2005 (p. 33) explicitly puts tone outside its scope and (pp. 230-231) treats penultimate accent only as an untested hypothesis borrowed from Meinhof 1932. Kanana Erastus 2011 describes segments and vowel length of six dialects but is silent on tone and stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Tiania (= Tigania, Glottolog dialect tiga1244), one of the six dialects Glottolog lists under meru1245, from the speech of co-author Mbûûi (Ming'ong'ine village, Tiania West). Ford 1976 independently confirms lexical tone for Imenti (imen1238), Tigania (tiga1244) and Miitine (miut1238) with named informants. Note: PHOIBLE's 'Kimeru (GM 1641)' inventory mapped to meru1245 cites Rubanza 2008 'Kimeru' (Languages of Tanzania Project) = Meru of Tanzania (Rwa), a different language; do not treat it as a meru1245 source.

sources.citation: Marete, Gideon Nteere. 1981. A study of grammatical agreement in Kimeru syntax: A transformational approach. MA thesis, University of Nairobi.
sources.note: Repository file is only the 3-page title/abstract; full thesis not online. Later theses cite it for the 7-vowel system and noun classes, not for tone or stress.

sources.citation: PHOIBLE inventory 'Kimeru (GM 1641)' and Grambank language page for meru1245 (accessed 2026-09-17).
sources.note: PHOIBLE cites Rubanza 2008 'Kimeru' (Languages of Tanzania Project) — Meru of Tanzania, not this language; no tone segments listed. Grambank lists Benson & Mburea 1966, Hodges 1977, Kinoti 1984 as sources; no stress feature.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Meru language' (accessed 2026-09-17).
sources.note: Consonant and vowel tables with vowel length; nothing on tone or stress; cites Kanana Erastus 2011.

sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M. & Mwaambi G. Mbûûi. 2023. The anterior-passive portmanteau suffix in Tiania. Studies in African Linguistics 52 (Suppl. 13): 7-17.
sources.note: No stress statement; p. 8 describes verb tone melodies (H from second mora to final/penult/antepenult, penult superhigh, final L) in Tiania. Morphology paper.

sources.citation: Kanana, Regina. 2016. Reduplication in Kimeru: A case study of Kimeru parts of speech. MA thesis, University of Nairobi.
sources.note: Section 2.2 lists seven vowels with long counterparts (citing Fr. Giorgis 1964 tentative Kimeru dictionary, Gacunku 2005, Marete 1981); nothing on tone or stress.

sources.citation: Taitumu, Bernard. 2014. Kimeru word-formation processes: An onomasiological approach. MA thesis, University of Nairobi.
sources.note: Section 2.1 gives consonant chart and seven vowels each with a long counterpart (pp. 28-29); no tone or stress description. p. 12, illustrating Štekauer's model with a coined Kimeru noun, says 'stress is placed on the first syllable of the new naming unit' (mwitithiangari) — an unargued aside, not a description.

sources.citation: Anondo, Timothy K. 2013. Open source spelling checker for Kîmîîrû language. MSc project, University of Nairobi.
sources.note: pp. 9-10 (citing Ataya 2012 on the new Kîmîîrû orthography): 'Like all other Bantu languages Kîmîîrû is highly tonal with every syllable having its own tone'; tone marks distinguish future negative commands from affirmatives; no stress statement. Computer-science project, not a linguistic description.

sources.citation: Kanana, Fridah Erastus. 2011. Meru dialects: The linguistic evidence. Nordic Journal of African Studies 20(4): 300-327.
sources.note: Silent on stress and tone; section 2 gives consonant and vowel systems of Imenti, Igoji, Mwimbi, Muthambi, Tharaka, Chuka and phonemic vs. phonetic vowel length (pp. 301-303); dialect boundaries argued from segmental, morphological and lexical features.

sources.citation: Gacunku, Lucyline. 2005. A phonological investigation of irregularity and variation in the Kimeru nominal concordial system. MA thesis, University of Nairobi.
sources.note: No stress rule. p. 33: 'Aspects of tone however are outside our scope in this study.' pp. 230-231 (recommendations): only segmental phonemes treated; quotes Meinhof 1932 on Ur-Bantu 'dynamic accent, which usually falls on the penultimate' and suggests stress allocation might explain Kimeru vowel lowering, calling these 'mere hypotheses that are still untested'.

sources.citation: Ford, Kevin C. 1976. Tone in Kikamba and the Central Kenya Bantu languages. Studies in African Linguistics 7(3): 261-293.
sources.note: No stress statement. p. 261: 'In all the dialects, tone is both lexically distinctive and serves to reinforce particular aspects of syntax'; dialects examined include Imenti, Tigania, Miitine (Meru), Mwimbi, Muthambi, Cuka, Tharaka, Embu, Mbeere, Kikuyu, Kikamba, with named informants (p. 262 n. 1). p. 267 (9): noun tonal classes by final tone: Tigania 5 classes, Miitine and one Imenti speaker 4, Tharaka and another Imenti speaker 3. Penultimate gliding rules (pp. 266-267) are stated for Kikamba only.
